clue.text: Has delinquent trimmed off a little bit of cash in this?

definitions.text: Has delinquent trimmed off a little bit of cash in this?

indicators.note: in tells us the small sum is placed inside the rearranged letters
off describes something gone wrong or bad, so the letters it governs are rearranged
trimmed tells us to pare the word delinquent at both ends, two letters from the front and two from the back

parts.note: a mite is a tiny amount, as in the widow's mite

indicators.note: a bit of the word cash is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: A sly embezzler shaves tiny amounts of money off accounts, and the clue asks what such a scheme is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trimmed' pares two letters from each end, leaving LINQUE; 'off' scrambles it with the first word, and 'in' sets the small sum inside. Read whole, the clue also describes the fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a fraud where minute sums are sliced from many transactions, just as the clue describes.

clue.text: Makes fun of sentences

definitions.meaning: jails a convict, in informal usage

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to parody someone and, colloquially, to commit someone to prison.

clue.text: Many informal things knocked down area

parts.note: lots are items sold under the auctioneer's hammer

explanation.surface: An auction scene where lots of items are knocked down to bidders in some area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'informal' is part of the definition: it marks the slangy spelling of 'lots of'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a casual, slangy spelling of 'lots of', meaning a great many.

clue.text: Demonstrate competitive people gathering to get a taste of really strong ale

parts.note: to demonstrate is to march in protest
a bee is a gathering for a contest, like a spelling bee

indicators.note: a taste is only a little, here the opening letter of the word really

explanation.surface: Protesters marching and rivals gathering, all for a sip of some very potent ale.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a historical name for an especially strong ale brewed in the month of March.

clue.text: Mastermind behind epic sport chasing cash receiver up

indicators.note: chasing means coming after, so this piece is placed second
in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a slot is where coins go in a machine
to sport with something is to toy with it

explanation.surface: A sports fan chases a cash machine upwards, oddly linked to the brains behind an epic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian novelist wrote War and Peace, the epic novel, so he is its mastermind.

clue.text: New World resident's found wife swinging, strangled by rope

indicators.note: being strangled by a rope means being wrapped inside it, so the cord goes around

parts.note: a cord is a thin rope
swinging, in the sense of sexually liberal, gives bi for bisexual

explanation.surface: A lurid tabloid tale: someone's wife found swinging, then strangled with a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an American bird, so it lives in the New World.

clue.text: Is leaving official meeting over smells

indicators.note: leaving says these letters depart from the word they sit in
over signals the meeting word is turned round

parts.note: a session is a formal sitting of a court or council

explanation.surface: Someone walks out once an official meeting is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns SESSION into NOISSES; 'leaving' removes IS from it.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to sniff something out is to detect its scent, so these are synonyms.

clue.text: Old Beatles number written after Queen proposal to drop intro

indicators.note: written after places this piece at the end
dropping the intro means losing the opening letter of the proposal phrase

parts.note: the words of a marriage proposal: 'marry me'

explanation.surface: A music quiz: an old Beatles number, a Queen song and a marriage proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to drop intro' removes M from MARRY ME, leaving ARRY ME; 'written after' puts N at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: This skiffle group, formed by John Lennon, became the Beatles, so it is the band's earlier name.

clue.text: Rare sense required to stop island getting plant disease

indicators.note: stopping a gap means plugging it, so one piece fills the other

parts.note: an eyot (or ait) is a small island in a river, a British word
ESP, extrasensory perception, is the rare sixth sense

explanation.surface: Someone with a rare sense is needed to save an island from a plant disease.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a fungal infection of cereals and other crops that leaves eye-like lesions.

clue.text: Real ivory

definitions.meaning: a white key on a piano, one played with no sharp or flat

explanation.definitionFit: The word means genuine, and in music it also names a white piano key, the old ivories.

clue.text: Holding a party to which girls aren't invited, we'll realise loss!

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the other letters sit inside

parts.words: party to which girls aren't invited
parts.note: a stag party is a men-only night out before a wedding

explanation.surface: A boys-only party that someone predicts will end in regret.
explanation.definitionFit: This means waste or loss, as of material or staff over time.

clue.text: What may hold up top saver's heading straight at PEP, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone awry, so these letters are scrambled
the heading of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A thrifty saver heads straight for a PEP, a type of UK investment plan, with bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: PEP was a Personal Equity Plan, a British tax-free savings scheme; 'unfortunately' rearranges S with STRAIGHT AT PEP.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a thin shoulder band supporting a dress or vest, holding up a garment's top.

clue.text: See 11
Encourage one back to look nosily around farm

indicators.note: around tells us the snooping word wraps the other letters

parts.note: to pry is to look nosily into others' affairs

indicators.note: back says the encourage-plus-one piece reads in reverse

parts.note: to egg on is to encourage
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Urging someone to snoop about a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' gives IGGE; 'around' wraps the snooping word round it.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a farm or pen where pigs are kept.

clue.text: Soldier capturing a foul-mouthed old patriot

indicators.note: capturing means taking in, so the soldier encloses the other letters

parts.note: GI is an American private soldier
ribald means coarse or vulgar in speech

explanation.surface: A soldier captures a coarse-tongued veteran patriot.
explanation.definitionFit: The nineteenth-century Italian general led the unification of Italy and is a national hero.

clue.text: Mark boundaries of shop with German

parts.note: a deli is a delicatessen, a food shop
mit is the German word for with

explanation.surface: A German shop owner marking out the edges of the premises.
explanation.definitionFit: To set the limits of something is to fix or mark its boundaries.

clue.text: Wormlike meandering around Cumbria, finding one Lake after another

indicators.note: around tells us the two lakes sit on either side of the jumbled county
one after another means the same letter twice in a row

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for lake

indicators.note: meandering means winding about, so the county's letters wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A walker meandering around Cumbria, the Lake District county, finding lake after lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meandering' gives UMBRICA; 'around' sets a lake letter at each end.
explanation.definitionFit: This means resembling an earthworm, from the Latin lumbricus, worm; it also names small hand muscles.

clue.text: Backsliding brother of the compiler's received cut

indicators.note: backsliding means going backwards, so the assembled letters are read in reverse
received means taken in, so the compiler goes inside

parts.note: Brer is a dialect form of brother, as in Brer Rabbit
the compiler is the setter, who calls himself I

explanation.surface: The setter complains of a backsliding sibling who has taken a cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The dialect brother is the one of Brer Rabbit fame. 'received' sets the setter inside, and 'Backsliding' turns the whole lot round.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a joint of beef taken from the front of the ribs, a butcher's cut.

clue.text: Expected waster of time to get lost during ascent

indicators.note: in a down clue, an ascent reads the letters from bottom to top
getting lost means disappearing, so this letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who wastes time is expected to get lost on a climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get lost' drops T from WASTER, giving WASER; 'during ascent' reverses WASER OF.
explanation.definitionFit: To have predicted or anticipated something is to have seen it coming.

clue.text: Not the first to check school soup

indicators.note: not the first means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: to abort something is to halt or check it

explanation.surface: A school kitchen inspection where someone other than the first checks the soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not the first' removes A from ABORT.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a variant spelling of the Eastern European beetroot soup.

clue.text: Private number ringing me for something spicy

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so the private number surrounds me

parts.note: a PIN is a personal identification number, kept private
to can mean for, as in 'a toast to the bride'

explanation.surface: Someone rings with a private number to tip me off about something spicy.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a sweet red pepper, the kind used to stuff olives.

clue.text: Dickensian father punished and holding son for transgression

indicators.note: holding means keeping inside, so the father wraps the rest

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father

indicators.note: punished suggests being knocked about, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A Victorian father punishes his son for a misdeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'punished' gives DSNA; 'holding' sets it between the father's first two letters and his last. 'for transgression' only explains the punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the pompous, complacent gentleman in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend.

clue.text: A guest of David Dimbleby keeping your secret?

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the guest wraps the other word

parts.note: Dimbleby long hosted the BBC debate show Question Time, QT, so a guest is on QT
in Irish or casual idiom the stands for your, as in 'how's the wife?'

explanation.surface: A panellist on a TV debate show trusted to keep your secret.
explanation.walkthrough: Question Time is the BBC's weekly political panel show, long chaired by David Dimbleby; 'keeping' wraps the guest round the Irish-style possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means secretly or quietly, so it describes something kept secret.

clue.text: Mug, owing — but not the mamma and singer

parts.note: to mug someone is to rob them

indicators.note: but not says the following word is left out

parts.note: in the red means in debt, owing money
mamma is the anatomical term for the milk-producing gland, a bosom

explanation.surface: Someone is mugged and in debt, but it is not Mum who sings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mamma' looks like mother but is the anatomical word for the bosom. 'but not' removes THE from IN THE RED.
explanation.definitionFit: This songbird is a common British garden species, so it is a singer.

clue.text: Turned up dull brown colour that's barely showing?

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation for 'that is'

explanation.surface: A drab brown colour turns up, barely visible.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an informal word for a film or show featuring naked performers, a bare showing.

clue.text: See 21
Inner self held up during cross-examination

indicators.note: in a down clue, held up means lifted, so the letters read bottom to top
during says the letters sit within the long word that follows

explanation.surface: A witness's true self is exposed during a cross-examination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' points to AMINA inside 'cross-examination'; 'held up' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jungian psychology this Latin term means the soul or the inner personality.

clue.text: Kept by European under hat is a Roman coin

indicators.note: kept by means held inside, so the hat sits within

parts.note: sous is the French, so European, word for under
lid is slang for a hat

explanation.surface: A Roman coin hidden under a European's hat.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the gold coin of the late Roman Empire, introduced by Constantine.

clue.text: French citizen one business is settling in Tyne and Wear?

indicators.note: settling in means moving inside, so these letters go within the region's letters

parts.note: Tyne and Wear is a county in North East England, so an example of NE
I is the Roman numeral one
Co is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: A Frenchman setting up a business in Tyne and Wear, the Newcastle area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'settling in' wraps the region round the rest; the question mark flags Tyne and Wear as only one example of the North East.
explanation.definitionFit: This means a native of Nice, so it is a citizen of that French city.

clue.text: Feature of old market place sadly trails contemporary in growth

indicators.note: in tells us these letters go inside the growth

parts.note: a wart is a small growth on the skin

indicators.note: trails means follows behind, so this piece comes second

parts.note: hi-tech means using up-to-date technology, so modern

indicators.note: sadly suggests things gone wrong, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An old market place sadly falls behind modern developments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' gives APELC; 'trails' sets it after the modern word, and 'in' puts both inside the growth.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the flat-bedded, two-wheeled vehicle used at Whitechapel hay market in old London.
